title: Great-grandfather's advice
hookLine: from his great-grandfather: good teachers at home, and spare no cost on them (Meditations 1.4)

lines: THE BEST MONEY SPENT ON YOU.
cards: What's the best money anyone ever spent on you? Not the biggest gift. The one that kept paying.
For a lot of people, it's a lesson: the piano teacher a grandparent paid for, the tutor that got you through chemistry, the swim class that means you can still save yourself in deep water.
Book one of the Meditations is Marcus's list of debts, one person at a time, and the fourth entry is about exactly this kind of spending.

teach.h: NO PUBLIC SCHOOL; GOOD TEACHERS AT HOME.
teach.b: First, the line. Section four is one sentence.

From his great-grandfather, Marcus says, he learned not to go to the public schools, to have good teachers at home, and, in the old Long translation, to know "that on such things a man should spend liberally." That's all.
Scholars usually identify him as Catilius Severus, an important senator on his mother's side of the family; exactly how the two were related is still debated.
Marcus was a boy from a rich and powerful family, and it shows. Third, be honest about it.
This is a wealthy household's advice. Most children in Rome never had a tutor at all, and many never learned to read.
But underneath it is a principle anyone can hold: education is worth spending on, generously, even when it costs. Fourth, look at what follows.
Of book one's seventeen entries, a great many are teachers: a painting teacher, a teacher of grammar, a teacher of rhetoric, several philosophers.
Marcus remembers each one by what they taught him to be, not just what they taught him to know: patience, plain speech, steadiness.
And spending isn't only money. It's time with someone who knows more than you, the humility to be corrected, a library card, a mentor's hour, a class you're nervous about.
His great-grandfather left him one sentence, and it's worth keeping.

how: Readers who take this line to heart often set aside money or time each year for learning: books, classes, or time with a mentor.

games.q: you're Marcus's great-grandfather, a rich senator, deciding how the boy should be taught. what do you advise?
o: send him to the public schools with everyone else.
good teachers at home, and spend freely on them.
teach him yourself, to save money.
games.why: good teachers at home, and spend liberally on such things. Marcus wrote it down decades later.

practice: Think of one teacher who shaped you, in school or out of it: a coach, a grandparent, a boss, an author. Picture them, and ask what they taught you to be, not only to know.
Then think of one thing you'd like to learn now, and what it would cost you in money, time or pride.
